Table \ref{tab:rmuclpooled} pools every Champions League season with possession data and reports Real Madrid's gaps per 10 matches, with intervals clustered by season and $t$ criticals on 18 degrees of freedom; the sample is 218 Real Madrid matches in 19 seasons, with the same matches behind the raw, pre-match and style-adjusted columns. For net yellow cards, the style-adjusted gap is $-2.39$ cards per 10 matches (95 percent CI $-5.66$ to $0.87$), equal in magnitude to 12 percent of the non-elite rate of 1.98 per match, and statistically indistinguishable from zero; the pre-match estimate is $-1.91$, and the gap relative to the other elite clubs is $-1.95$ (95 percent CI $-4.35$ to $0.45$, $p = 0.105$). For net fouls, the style-adjusted gap is $6.40$ fouls per 10 matches (95 percent CI $-6.70$ to $19.49$), equal in magnitude to 5 percent of the non-elite rate of 13.22 per match, and statistically indistinguishable from zero; the pre-match estimate is $6.64$, and the gap relative to the other elite clubs is $12.89$ (95 percent CI $2.25$ to $23.54$, $p = 0.020$). For net penalties, the style-adjusted gap is $-0.23$ penalties per 10 matches (95 percent CI $-1.44$ to $0.98$), equal in magnitude to 17 percent of the non-elite rate of 0.14 per match, and statistically indistinguishable from zero; the pre-match estimate is $-0.01$, and the gap relative to the other elite clubs is $-0.64$ (95 percent CI $-1.61$ to $0.33$, $p = 0.180$). For net red cards, the style-adjusted gap is $0.22$ red cards per 10 matches (95 percent CI $-0.80$ to $1.24$), equal in magnitude to 23 percent of the non-elite rate of 0.10 per match, and statistically indistinguishable from zero; the pre-match estimate is $0.43$, and the gap relative to the other elite clubs is $0.40$ (95 percent CI $-0.42$ to $1.21$, $p = 0.322$). Conditional on the fouls called, the net yellow-card gap is $-2.98$ cards per 10 matches (95 percent CI $-5.43$ to $-0.53$), statistically significant at the five percent level. Dropping the 8 Real Madrid matches that went to extra time moves the net yellow-card estimate to $-2.34$ and the net penalty estimate to $-0.35$.

A null is informative only in proportion to what the sample could detect, so Figure \ref{fig:rmuclprecision} traces precision as seasons accumulate. Pooled over all seasons, the design detects, with 80 percent power, a net yellow-card gap of $4.60$ cards per 10 matches (23 percent of the non-elite rate) and a net penalty gap of $1.71$ penalties per 10 matches (124 percent); a single season resolves roughly $10.22$ cards and $3.37$ penalties at the same confidence. The 90 percent intervals rule out net yellow-card gaps beyond $5.09$ cards and net penalty gaps beyond $1.23$ penalties per 10 matches in either direction; these are equivalence margins against stated bounds, not evidence of no bias. Figure \ref{fig:rmuclstability} shows that the pooled estimates do not rest on one season: leaving out each season in turn moves the net yellow-card gap across net yellow cards ($-3.13$ to $-1.69$; the refits straddle the five percent boundary), net fouls across net fouls ($3.04$ to $9.13$; every refit covers zero), and net penalties across net penalties ($-0.51$ to $0.10$; every refit covers zero). The season estimates themselves are more dispersed than sampling noise alone implies for net yellow cards (heterogeneity $Q$ test $p = 0.03$, $I^2 = 43$ percent, between-season standard deviation $3.77$ cards per 10 matches with an upper bound of $6.89$), which is why the shrunk season estimates in the figure sit close to the pooled line; their intervals condition on the estimated between-season variance and are model-based rather than design-based.
